narrative:
The model determined that you have a 63.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is substantially lower than the average of roughly 6 among students who were accepted, signaling that your later academic performance raised serious concerns about your readiness for the bar.

Your LSAT score of 36 was the second most important factor. Although this score is only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, it still nudged the prediction modestly toward passing. Unfortunately, this positive effect was not large enough to offset the other signals.

Your first-year class ranking came in third. Placing in the second decile (well below the average of 6 among accepted students) added further weight toward predicting failure.

Taken together, your consistently lower academic standing in law school, especially in the later years, outweighed the relatively solid LSAT result and led the model to conclude you are more likely than not to fail the bar.

What you should do next is focus on improving your academic performance if you retake courses or consider programs with additional bar-preparation support. Strengthening your upper-level grades and raising your LSAT score would be the most direct ways to change this outcome in a future application. (248 words)
